newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Brief relief from retail sales?.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Brief relief from retail sales?.

text.p: Investors will receive a double-dose of top-tier data on Friday and U.S. analysts said Treasury prices could get some temporary relief.
The Commerce Department is scheduled to release its March retail sales report at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT and the Labor Department will issue its report on March producer prices simultaneously.
With producer prices expected to remain subdued, analysts said market reaction would hinge on the retail sales report.
On average, economists polled by Reuters forecast retail sales to have risen 0.6 percent in March and by 0.4 percent in the month excluding automobile sales.

Matthew Alexy, chief markets strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston, said that even if the retail sales report is benign, market participants are not ready to view the economy as cooling. But he did say that bonds had room to rise on the report.
"We are at the cheap end of the trading range," Alexy said. "You may have a little bit of a migration (lower in yield) on the long bond," he said.
For the long bond to rally, non-automobile sales would have to print 0.2 percent or lower, analysts said. Over the past three months, the non-automobile sales had an average gain of 0.7 percent.

"Given that this data was so important a month ago, you could easily imagine a softer growth profile leading to a rally in bonds," said Chris Rupkey, vice president and financial economist at BOT/Mitsubishi, who forecast retail sales o have risen 0.5 percent.

Looking at PPI, Wall Street analysts predicted an unchanged headline figure in March after a 0.4 percent decline in February. Excluding volatile food and energy components, PPI was seen rising 0.1 percent against a 0.1 percent dip in the previous month.

"The chances are (PPI) will come in subdued again," said Peter Kretzmer, senior economist at NationsBanc Capital Markets Inc. Kretzmer said the upside for the report is pretty limited. "Something that would really grab the market would be an ex-food and energy finished goods change of above 0.3 percent," he said, referring to the downside.
In addition to the data, analysts said the market will also keep their eye on two senior Federal Reserve officials who are scheduled to speak on Friday.

Federal Reserve Vice Chair Alice Rivlin will discuss issues relating to balancing the budget at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT and Richmond Federal Reserve President Alfred Broaddus is set to speak at 1200 EDT/1600 GMT in Virginia.

Late Thursday afternoon, two-year notes were off 1/32 at 99-21/32, yielding 6.44 percent. Ten-year notes were down 1/32 at 95-12/32 to yield 6.90 percent. The 30-year bellwether bond was off 1/32 at 94-02/32, yielding 7.11 percent.
